stimulus: Historian Kim Wagner ('The Deconstructed Stranglers,' 2004) reexamines the British campaign against 'thuggee' — alleged gangs who robbed and strangled travelers in early-1800s India in the name of the goddess Kali. Wagner argues that the British official William Sleeman, who led the campaign in the 1830s, built his account on inconsistencies and exaggerations, presenting thuggee as a vast, organized menace partly to advance his own standing within the colonial administration.

explanation: The standard story — brave Britons suppressing the murderous thugs — cast empire as a rescue mission bringing order to a chaotic India. If the danger was largely invented, that justification collapses: the 'rescue' was solving a problem the British had exaggerated.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The thuggee campaign was Exhibit A for the claim that empire brought order; Wagner removes the exhibit.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The thuggee narrative was about lawlessness, not about princes' attitudes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The campaign was never presented as an economic achievement.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The thuggee story concerned crime, not religious conflict.
